title: Control Flow
summary: Make decisions with if/else and switch, repeat work with for, while, do-while and range-based for, and control loops with break and continue.
introduction: Programs are interesting because they choose and repeat. C++ offers the same branching and looping statements as C, Java and JavaScript, plus two modern refinements: an `if` that declares its own variable and a range-based `for` that walks any container without index arithmetic. This lesson shows each statement with a small program, then uses them together for the classic FizzBuzz and a loop that needs an early exit.
learningObjectives: Write if/else chains and the C++17 if-with-initialiser form
Use switch correctly, including break and intentional fallthrough
Choose between for, while, do-while and range-based for
Control a loop with break and continue

blocks.text: An `if` statement runs its block when the condition is `true`. Conditions are usually comparisons (`<`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`) combined with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not). Any numeric value also works as a condition: zero is false, everything else is true, which is why `if (count)` means "if count is not zero". Since C++17 an `if` can declare a variable in an initialiser section; the variable is visible in both branches and nowhere else, which keeps temporary names from leaking into the rest of the function.

blocks.title: grade.cpp

blocks.text: Always write the braces, even for a single statement. `if (x) doThis(); doThat();` runs `doThat()` unconditionally, and the indentation will lie to you.

When you compare one integer or character against several constant values, `switch` reads better than a chain of `else if`. Execution jumps to the matching `case` label and then **keeps going** until it meets a `break`, so every case normally ends with one. `default` handles everything else.

blocks.title: calculator.cpp
Common mistake: the missing break
blocks.text: Leave out the `break` after `case '+':` and a `+` would print the sum **and then** the product, because control falls through into the next case. Compilers warn about this with `-Wimplicit-fallthrough` (part of `-Wextra`). When you genuinely want two cases to share code, write the labels back to back (`case 'a': case 'A':`) or mark the fall-through with `[[fallthrough]];` so readers and the compiler know it is intentional. A related slip is `if (x = 5)` instead of `if (x == 5)`: the first assigns 5 and is always true; `-Wall` warns, and some teams write `if (5 == x)` to make the typo a compile error.

The classic `for` loop has three parts: an initialiser, a condition checked before every iteration, and a step. The **range-based** `for` (`for (int t : temperatures)`) walks every element of a container, array or string without an index, which removes the off-by-one errors that indexed loops invite. Use the classic form when you need the index itself or a step other than one.

blocks.title: fizzbuzz.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra fizzbuzz.cpp -o fizzbuzz
$ ./fizzbuzz
1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz Fizz 7 8 Fizz Buzz 11 Fizz 13 14 FizzBuzz
average: 23.75

blocks.text: Two details: the test for 15 must come first, because a multiple of 15 is also a multiple of 3, and `condition ? a : b` is the conditional operator, an expression that picks one of two values; here it prints a space between numbers and a newline after the last one. `std::vector` is the standard growable array; the [containers lesson](/tutorials/cpp/stl-containers) covers it fully.

`while` repeats as long as its condition holds and is the right choice when you do not know the iteration count in advance. `do ... while` checks the condition *after* each pass, so the body always runs at least once, which suits "ask until the input is valid" loops. Inside any loop, `continue` skips to the next iteration and `break` leaves the loop entirely.

blocks.title: loops.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra loops.cpp -o loops
$ ./loops
27 reaches 1 in 111 steps
1
3
5
7
attempts: 3

The count is unknown; possibly zero iterations
The body must run at least once (input validation)
One integer or char compared against several constants

blocks.title: Prefer ++i
blocks.text: `++i` and `i++` both add one, but `i++` must keep a copy of the old value to return it. For `int` the compiler optimises the difference away; for iterators it may not, so C++ programmers write `++i` by habit when the old value is not used.

questions.question: What does this loop print?
questions.explanation: `continue` skips the rest of the body when `i` is 2, so only 1, 3 and 4 are printed before the loop ends.

questions.question: The body of a `do ... while` loop always executes at least once.
questions.explanation: The condition is evaluated after the body, so the first pass happens regardless of the condition's value.
